This work introduces a functional analog to the volume of a convex body and develops the theory behind it, establishing functional equivalents of various inequalities in convex geometry. The functional analog leverages the concept of log-submodularity, which enables the derivation of multiple inequalities. Notable examples include functional versions of the Brunn-Minkowski and Brunn type inequalities, as well as a functional form of the logarithmic Minkowski inequality. Additionally, this theory has implications for the learning rate of a specific type of stochastic process, the online bandit MCMC. The connection between the two is established by demonstrating that the negative relative entropy between the process's state and its stationary distribution follows a submodular functional relationship. As a result, this theory provides a novel perspective on learning rate analysis in online bandit MCMC. The learning rate properties derived from this theory can be applied to a range of stochastic processes, both convex and concave, encompassing both Markov chain and diffusion models. Notably, this work provides the first unified treatment of convex stochastic processes, encompassing both discrete and continuous-time stochastic processes, as well as both Markov chain and diffusion models. The theory developed in this work is exemplified through the specific case of the online bandit Langevin diffusion, a specific type of stochastic differential equation that arises in the context of distributed and federated learning. The learning rate properties of this process are analyzed under various noise conditions, including the case of a non-convex diffusion with noise that follows a convex stochastic process, as well as the case of a convex diffusion with noise that follows a non-convex stochastic process. Notably, this work provides the first unified treatment of the learning rate of the stochastic process in the case of a non-convex diffusion with a convex noise and a non-convex noise respectively. The theoretical results are further validated through numerical experiments. The code for these experiments is provided at https://github.com/zhengqiuw/convex-functional-inequalities. The developed theory is also implemented in the Python package ConvexFunctionalInequalities, as part of the larger Python package ConvexOptimization. Experimental results on several real-world hyperspectral images demonstrate the superiority of the proposed MDAN method over state-of-the-art denoising techniques. Deep neural networks have been the driving force behind recent advancements in machine learning, and their success can be attributed to their ability to be expressed as deep artificial neural networks that mirror the structure of the human brain. This similarity allows for the application of principles rooted in psychology, notably the concept of equipping DNNs with "common sense" inference operators like causality and temporal inference. Empirical evidence suggests that incorporating these operators can lead to improved accuracy, and our research aims to build upon this understanding by exploring the impact of combining multiple inference operators in a single model. We conducted an experiment that involved training a model on a set of tasks that required different inferences and subsequently tested it on a separate, unseen task that demanded a unique combination of operators. Our results show that the model's performance on the test task was influenced by the specific combination of operators used during training, and we observed that the model's ability to generalize learned knowledge on unseen tasks varies significantly depending on how the different operators are combined. We also found that the application of certain inference operators can lead to overfitting, and we demonstrated that this issue can be mitigated by using a regularizer to reduce the model's reliance on specific inference paths. Our research provides insights into the impact of integrating multiple inference operators in deep neural networks and offers a framework for using these networks to simulate human-like reasoning abilities. We envision that our findings will contribute to the development of more intelligent AI systems that can better understand and apply the principles of human reasoning. The code and data used in our study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepCausalLearner/common-sense-inference. We plan to release the model and code for the regularizer soon. The rapid advancement of autonomous driving technology has seen a surge in interest for simulating driving scenarios. However, generating authentic driving scenes that reflect real-world conditions remains a challenge. To address this, researchers have developed a text-based approach to driving scene generation. Nevertheless, incorporating domain expertise to ensure the generation of realistic scenes remains an open issue. To resolve this, we introduce a framework that integrates domain knowledge into driving scene generation. By representing domain knowledge as a directed graph and using a hierarchical attention mechanism, our model can generate coherent driving scenes. We evaluate our approach through both qualitative and quantitative assessments, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing scenes that conform to real-world traffic patterns and safety regulations. Furthermore, our results show that the proposed hierarchical attention mechanism outperforms random sampling in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Finally, we examine the impact of domain expertise on the quality of generated scenes, highlighting the potential for further improvements in this area. We investigate how an external control system affects the growth of tissue cells utilizing a mathematical model that accounts for cell proliferation and cell cycle progression. Our study reveals that the dynamics of tissue growth can be manipulated by adjusting key parameters of the control system, particularly in regards to the timing and intensity of external influences, leading to two distinct growth patterns: accelerated and retarded growth. Furthermore, we examine how the balance between these opposing growth patterns impacts the development of patterning in tissue as it expands. Our findings indicate that the organization of tissue structure is highly sensitive to the cell population density and the timing of external control applications. Interestingly, we observed that the organization of tissue structure exhibits a critical transition at a specific density, characterized by a non-standard power-law behavior. We present a groundbreaking approach to estimating a 3D head model from a single portrait image, known as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). By utilizing a meta-learning framework, our method enables the rapid adaptation of a pre-trained neural network to new images, resulting in highly detailed and accurate 3D models. Our approach achieves this by leveraging a two-part optimization process that includes pre-training a network to estimate NeRF parameters and then applying that knowledge to estimate new images, leading to significantly improved 3D head reconstruction from a single portrait. Our method's efficacy is evident in its ability to outperform existing techniques by accurately estimating 3D models from a wide range of head shots, including low-resolution and in-depth images, as well as images with varying lighting conditions and from novel viewpoints. Moreover, our method's robustness to different image types is demonstrated by its ability to estimate 3D models from images with sunglasses, hats, and other obstructions. We also show that our method's 3D head models can be successfully used for real-time head reconstruction, allowing for the transfer of a 3D head model to a new image, and for the generation of photorealistic head shots in a 3D environment. Our results highlight the potential of meta-learning to improve the performance of NeRF-based 3D head reconstruction from a single portrait. Soft continuum body robots can be modeled as flexible rods to navigate their environment, with the Piecewise Constant Curvature (PCC) model being widely used due to its simplicity. The proposed estimator is then compared to traditional methods, such as the least-squares algorithm, through both simulated and real-world experiments. Furthermore, the proposed estimator is shown to be a valuable tool for accurately navigating and avoiding obstacles in complex environments. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of more accurate models for soft continuum body robots, enabling them to navigate their environment with greater precision and accuracy. In the context of computational design, procedural generation is a key concept that allows for the creation of intricate designs through automated processes. While this concept has been extensively researched, its practical application in creating complex, interactive products with a need for continuous design flexibility has been less explored. To bridge this gap, a new procedural growth approach for interior architecture is introduced, enabling the automatic generation of highly customizable rooms with multiple configurations. The proposed method utilizes a simplified procedural model, the Wave Function Collapse algorithm, that can be easily extended to accommodate diverse design requirements. An empirical study of 200 randomly generated rooms is conducted to assess the effectiveness of different configuration settings, yielding valuable insights into design flexibility and procedural generation. The findings demonstrate that procedural generation is a viable tool for designers, even when working with highly constrained design spaces. Moreover, this approach facilitates the creation of design alternatives, enabling users to explore different design paths during the interactive design process. The design system is implemented in a computational design tool, illustrating how procedural generation can enhance design flexibility and streamline the room layout generation process. The study's outcomes provide valuable insights into procedural generation in computational design and offer a novel perspective on the design exploration process. Although formal synthesis tools provide a solution, their generated controllers are often unverifiable due to limitations in formal proof methods. To address this issue, we have developed a framework that utilizes the D-FP tool to construct proofs for the safety of controllers, derived from synthesis using the SCOTS tool. By integrating both systems, we aim to streamline the process of constructing comprehensive evidence for controller safety. To demonstrate the practical value of our approach, we have successfully proven the safety of a controller for a model of a high-temperature annealer, derived from a real-world machine design. This novel application showcases the potential benefits for various safety-critical fields, where rigorous proof construction can significantly enhance trust in control systems. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of synthesizing a controller and its supporting proof from a single machine model, paving the way for broader applications in safety-critical systems. This research introduces innovative metrics, opinion diversity and active links density,
to assess polarization levels within social networks. We employ these metrics in
a simulated environment by modeling the evolution of opinions within a dynamic
social network. The process of opinion formation occurs through a complex system
where agents interact with multiple influencers and randomly selected peers. As
influencers' opinions shift, agents with flexible responses adapt in sympathy or
opposition, while new social connections form and disappear based on
interactions. We then examine how polarization develops over time in relation
to varying factors: agents' ability to adapt, the rate of social connections
changing, and the distribution of influencers' initial opinions. The results show
that polarization arises in networks with diverse adaptive capabilities and
dynamic connections, while uniform adaptation and frequent social interactions can
lead to uniform opinions. Conversely, polarization decreases in networks with
uniform active connections and limited social exchange. These findings provide
insights into the complex system's behavior and highlight the importance of
flexible responses and social connections in mitigating extreme opinions. We
believe that these metrics can be applied to real-world scenarios, such as
social media platforms, to better understand and address polarization. The

temporally annotated action labels to teach video-grounded reasoning, 
accompanied by a modular design that incorporates video encoding and dynamic control elements.

We analyze two instances of flawed derivations, related to the van der Waals model and the quantum theory of magnetism, and present correct alternatives. In contrast to common practice, we affirm that mathematicians cannot anticipate the need for their expertise in reviewing papers; instead, the reviewer must be a skilled mathematician. We also touch upon other mathematical errors present in Landau's works and provide supporting resources, specifically the companion lecture notes available for free digital download. In an effort to prevent similar errors, we highlight changes that should be made when converting mathematical derivations to educational textbooks format. This research presents a novel approach to long-term human motion capture in AR,
utilizing a wearable IMU-LIDAR system that enables accurate pose estimation.
Our method enhances precision by integrating IMU data with LiDAR point cloud
features, and demonstrates improved performance in AR applications where IMU
provides short-term and global pose information while LIDAR supplies robust
local features. Our results indicate a significant improvement in tracking error
for a single camera AR setup, reducing the average pose error by 26.2% and the
average hand pose error by 35.3% in comparison to IMU-only and LiDAR-only
methods, and maintaining its accuracy even after 30 minutes. Our research also
highlights the benefits of combining IMU and LIDAR data for human motion tracking.

This research presents a groundbreaking approach to anomaly detection, which identifies novel, previously unseen classes in a given dataset. It achieves this by utilizing a one-class classifier to distinguish between samples from familiar classes and those from unknown classes. However, the generation of novel samples for the unknown class is challenging due to the lack of knowledge about the unknown class. Traditional methods often rely on the available labeled samples from familiar classes. In contrast, our proposed Optimal Perturbation Generation (OPG) method generates high-quality samples for the unknown class by leveraging the available labeled samples from familiar classes. We formulate the generation process as a constrained optimization problem that minimizes the classification loss of the novel samples for the one-class classifier. We also introduce a novel loss function, which penalizes samples that are similar to those from familiar classes. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed OPG method outperforms existing anomaly detection methods, which are evaluated on a variety of benchmark datasets. Additionally, we conduct a detailed analysis of the proposed OPG method, which is shown to be robust and efficient. The code for training and testing our proposed method is available on the GitHub repository "OPG-anomaly-detection". We introduce a novel cost constructor that can handle occlusions and create a complete cost map at every depth estimation step, which is essential for optimization-based monocular depth estimation. Our approach uses a generative adversarial network to predict a complete cost map, including not only the direct depth matches but also occluded pixels, thus eliminating the need for iterative optimization and reducing propagation errors. Additionally, our method can learn to adapt to different types of occlusions using limited annotated data, demonstrating promising results in monocular depth estimation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets and find that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in monocular depth estimation.
